author: reek
body: Before this, the boot processor was the only core with a clock. The PIT's interrupt is delivered to it alone, and an AP was started with interrupts disabled and no timer of its own, so a process that never yielded owned the core it was given until it exited. Each AP now arms its own local APIC timer and unmasks interrupts, so a scheduling tick arrives on every core.

author: reek
body: The boot processor's id is always zero, and nothing on its path -- and no host code -- writes that cell. So a value above zero is not evidence that the children finished, and it is not evidence that an AP ran them. It is evidence that a core other than the boot processor took a scheduling clock tick, which is the thing that makes it preemptible.

author: reek
body: The distinction is the whole point of the test. Six children finishing proves nothing: one core does that. Even six children finishing ON six cores proves nothing about preemption -- an AP that runs its child to completion undisturbed has still never been preempted. The claim is about who can be interrupted, so the evidence has to be about who was interrupted.

author: reek
body: The spin is long on purpose, and the margin is deliberate. A scheduling tick arrives every few tens of milliseconds, so a child that finishes in less than that is never a candidate for preemption on any core: the test would report NO AP WAS PREEMPTED while the machinery underneath worked perfectly. The first cut of this test did exactly that -- the whole guest ran in under a single tick period.

author: reek
body: The second cut was worse, because it passed. It ran for two or three tick periods, which is enough to be preempted and not enough to be sure of it, and at eight cores -- where the children run more in parallel and the whole thing finishes sooner -- it failed one run in three. A test whose result depends on winning a race against the clock it is measuring is not a test. The spin is now long enough that every core takes many ticks.
